title: Embouchure, reed strength and Tio's own reed
summary: Tio taught lip over bottom teeth and upper teeth on the mouthpiece but allowed variation; reeds varied.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Now, did he say anything about your mouthpiece or your reeds? For instance, do you put your teeth on the upper part of the mouthpiece or do you use just your lips on there?
Well, the way I was trained, he had to hold my lip kind of tight on the bottom with the teeth done.
Yeah. Teeth covered on the bottom? Yeah. Against the reed.

The lip. No. The lip covering the teeth. Uh-huh. And the upper teeth on the mouthpiece. The upper teeth on the mouthpiece. On the mouthpiece. Oh. He said, now, of course, that's the way I was taught. He said, but those kind of things, they vary. It depends on the individual sometimes. He said, you may take it and always have a bite like that and it may come a time when you don't want a bite. So, truthfully speaking, you notice I don't have the malk like most of them have. Yeah. I probably say, well, but it kind of worried me a while. Uh-huh. And you take, they have a lot of clarinets that they- Clared down. They're wearing it out. Because Teo's was partly worn himself, you see. And he did have the bite, but I never did really get myself accustomed to really biting with my upper teeth.
No. That's what I thought when I watched you play, you seemed to have more pressure with your lip.

Yeah. That's right. I never did. Because he told me that's the way he was taught. He thought that was the proper way. He said, but you can't go by those things because he said, there's so many others that can get so much out of instruments and they violate rules and regulations. So he said, whatever way you can get the best result and the way it sounded to me, I'll let it go at that. Uh-huh.
What about the reed? Did you use a hard reed or a soft reed or-

Well, in the beginning I used a very soft reed. But then it was too reedy, he claimed. It wasn't getting the sound that he thought would be best. Uh-huh. So he told me to use a little stiffer reed. And then it depended on the way my amateur came. Now sometimes I can use a much stiffer reed and other times I'll have to switch to a soft reed. It depends just the way my mouth is.
What kind of teal used himself did he ever say? Mostly it was just about a medium hard.
It was a medium hard reed that he used. That would be about a number three nowadays, wouldn't it? Yeah, so. Uh-huh. Because in those days they weren't numbered anyway. That's right. I can say.
